MS. WILLARD: Hmmm. "The earliest jazz recorded on the West Coast was undoubtedly the three Nordskog recordings by Kid Ory; however, in the opinion of these writers, the leading lights in the recorded jazz music were Sonny Clay, Reb Spikes, and Harvey Brooks. Benjamin F. "Reb" Spikes and his brother Johnny, now deceased, were in the entertainment field as far back as 1911. They travelled with minstrel shows, ran theaters, played with numerous bands, wrote some very successful tunes and operated a highly popular music store. The music store was opened in 1919 at 1203 South Central Avenue in Los Angeles and soon became the mecca of all colored musicians in the area. Reb could and did furnish most any kind of band and for most any event. The store was probably the only outlet on the Coast for jazz and blues records issued by the major recording firms in the East. Reb often worked with Jelly Roll Morton during the latter's two visits to the West and enjoys telling stories about his association with Jelly. Reb also states that Morton definitely did no recording while there. However, the two did collaborate on several successful tunes. No doubt, Reb and Johnny's "Someday Sweetheart" was their biggest hit and is still paying royalties. Reb's only recording efforts were 'Sheffield's Blues,' 'Steppin' High' on Hollywood, as by... on Hollywood, as by Reb's Legion Club..."
Hollywood Boulevard, they mean.
Oh...didn't quite make sense... "...Reb's Legion Club Forty-Fives and 'My Mammy's Blues,' 'Fight That Thing' on Columbia as by Reb Spikes' Majors and Minors. He is currently engaged in the
real estate business in Los Angeles but still maintains his interest in music."
This is from what magazine?
I don't know. I didn't know all of that was in there. Or to tell you the truth, at least I forgot it.
I think one more page to the cover...oh, ...Jazz Monthly, May, 1961.
Who is that? Is that uh...?
Hmmm, "West Coast Jazz in the 20s, articles by John Bentley and Ralph W. Miller." Uh...
That looks like Royal. That is Royal.
Marshal?
Yeah, see him with his sax? See, this is 19-what?
'61, it says. Hmmm. Let's see if it...
Did we skip a page?
No, I just wondered whether it...whether it, uh ...it's an English magazine, Jazz Monthly. London office. Albert G. McCarthy, editor. That's the man that wrote that Big Bands book.
Is he? Well, I wonder, is that guy...he never said a word to me about it. I...I found it out by somebody else telling me about it.
The big bands book?
Yeah.
He's got an awful lot of information. I thought he must have been in touch with you.
